wa_accendo_lunae_lib_west_face_var.notes: Shared with Let it Burn and the West Face. A few steep moves up the broken ramp system trending right, past a tree, then easier ground to a flat ledge below a vertical splitter. Grades given for this pitch range from 5.7 to 5.8.
A short thin-hands splitter, roughly 25 ft of hard climbing, then easier ground up and left along the ledge to the trees at its far left end for the belay.

Finger cracks lead to a V-slot with a thin crack. The flakes on the left are detached: step on them rather than pull. Go up and right past a small roof, then traverse left past two bolts on the crux moves. Finish on knobs and a finger crack to a two-bolt belay. The old fixed pin is gone and leaves a good cam placement.
Hands and fingers on knobs, fins and thin cracks, stepping right twice into new crack systems, to a double crack. Belay at a fixed pin and a bolt on a small ledge.

Move into the right-slanting flared slot, mantle right onto a square ledge, then make a powerful layback past an overhanging flake. Near the top of this pitch Accendo Lunae leaves Let it Burn: belay on a bench to the right, on gear around 1 in.

New terrain. Traverse right, then climb a gently overhanging line of thin cracks and tips locks. The crux passes a wedged flake that flexes, so gear placements beside it are unreliable. Belay in a small alcove in the chimney just right of a razor-sharp flake. Grades for this pitch range from 5.11c to 5.12-.

New terrain. Awkward body positions up a tips crack in a V-shaped flare lead to a stance under a 4 ft roof where the corner switches from right-facing to left-facing. Good gear overhead protects a double hand-jam pull over the roof into thin hands, which fights up to a ledge. Grades given run from 5.11- to mid-5.11.
Back on the West Face for its crux: a perfect hand crack up the arching corner to an even bigger roof, surmounted on its left side to a stance. Grades range from 5.11c to 5.12-.

The West Face's overhanging chimneys. Fight past the first overhang into a squeeze chimney, exit to a crack, then into a second flaring chimney. Step right at a big block to belay on a large ledge. Originally rated 5.8, it is widely regarded as climbing like 5.10.

Easy blocky ground up and right to the summit, usually simul-climbed. A notch on the far right gives quick access to the walk-off. From the summit block a single 30 m rappel east off a slung horn reaches the descent.

wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.notes: Start as for The Tiger, then step right over a small tree onto a ledge that runs right and curves into a long left-facing corner. Climb the corner to a pin-and-gear belay under a roof that traverses back left. At least one of the pins has pulled out, so carry several RPs and small nuts to build a solid anchor.

The first crux. Get established with awkward stemming off slightly creaky holds in the corner, clip the bolt, then stem wide left, place a quick piece and dyno off poor holds to a huge bucket out left. The dyno is very temperature dependent. Mantle out and finish on slightly dirty 5.10 to a small stance up and left with a snag; belay on tips-to-finger cams high in the corner.

Traverse straight left off the belay to a crack system hidden from view, and follow it to the big treed ledge that splits the wall. The corner is dirty, but the crack itself hardly needs to be touched. At the top, either climb the crack directly above a small snag or take the easier line right, which adds rope drag.

The standout pitch. Walk right along the ledge to the clean right-facing flake. Climb moderate moves up the flake, then make a puzzling switch right into a second crack past a thin seam. Power up that crack to its end just below a bolt, then pull through strong moves on square-cut edges that ease above the bolt. Belay from a stopper and bolt.

Make an awkward move off the belay, then face climb on good gear up the crack above. Layback a somewhat mossy left-facing corner with clean jams until a horizontal crack leads far left into the largest cave on the wall. Belay on bolts at the end of the traverse; protect the traverse for the second.

Aim for the hanging left-facing flake above the cave lip. Climb up and left on easy but unprotected ground to a horizontal, follow it right into a corner, and climb up and left past some hollow flakes to a small roof, turning it on the left. From a ledge with a small tree, run out easy holds to the first gear in a short corner. Climb the tree to a higher ledge and belay on finger-to-hand cams.

Traverse the ledge system left as it narrows until you are forced into a hand traverse and some downclimbing, then follow flakes and ledges to join the upper Ellen Pea. Belay on bolts shortly after the two routes meet. A committing pitch for the second, who faces the same traverse with a fall that swings.

Finish on Ellen Pea's upper line. Climb up and right on hollow flakes to the first of three bolts, then make steep moves on good but grainy holds until the angle eases. Easier ground leads up and right to a treed ledge with a bolted anchor. From there, rappel Ellen Pea with two ropes, or continue up runout 5.9 edges to the top and walk off to the west.

wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.notes: Technical crux of the route: easy but unremarkable climbing up a left-slanting crack leads to a delicate 5.11- tips crux guarding a wide stem box, then a pumpy lieback in twin cracks.
The mental crux — committing slab stemming and technical fingerwork on an offset tips crack past a fixed pin, PG13 but never truly dangerous.
Stellar 5.10 corner climbing following an obvious flake/crack system.
Crack-switch moves and a committing 'wild pillar' mantel.
Short corner crux and slab climbing past a bulge to a small ledge.
Offsize splitter with a low crux, transitioning to perfect hands, then a chimney with a loose block before topping out.

or_european_vacation.notes: Starts up the bolted line of The Struggle Within, climbing a crack past its first four bolts, then steps right to the belay bolts beneath the second pitch of the East Wall route.
Bolted climbing that trends up and right to reach the arete followed by Eye of the Beholder. Pitches 1 and 2 can be linked on a 70 m rope if the rope is managed with long runners.
Easy natural-gear climbing at about 5.7 leads to one bolt-protected hard move, then a crack that widens up to a hanging belay. Pitches 3 and 4 can be linked on a 70 m rope with runners.
A wide crack taking 4-inch gear, then the line veers right to a bolted finish over a bulge. Belay on a ledge.
Easy bolted face climbing on imperfect rock up to an anchor. Pitches 5 and 6 can be linked on a 70 m rope.
A bolted face crosses a section of poor rock; the holds near the top are solid.

The finest climbing on the route, on solid rock near the top of the summit tower. Once at the arete, clip a bolt to protect the second, then move down and around the corner onto a ledge. The anchor there is not built for rappelling.
Move right to a water streak with bolts and stem up past questionable rock to a better finish. Belay on the slings or bolts just above the lip, or carry on to the summit and belay there.

wa_clean_break.notes: From a good ledge with a low fixed pin, climb the namesake splitter: a sustained thin-hands crack up clean, vertical white granite. It is the hardest pitch of the route; extra 0.5 and 0.75 cams help anyone without small hands. Parties sometimes retreat after this pitch, but the 5.10 pitches above are easier.

Skip the dirty right-facing corner and take the 3-inch crack up and right over a small roof, past a 4-inch horizontal, up a slab and over a second roof (about 5.10a). To keep it at 5.9, traverse left into the original corner instead of taking the second roof. Belay on a small ledge with a bushy tree.

Traverse briefly left, then climb a left-facing corner and angle right past a tree to belay at a horn. Published topos disagree on this section and on the next traverse, and parties commonly go off route in the first few pitches.

Go down and right only a short way from the belay (roughly 5 ft down and 15 ft right, not a long descent), then make an insecure move around the arete onto a ledge. Climb blocks to a belay beside a huge flake. Going left here, or down too far, leads off route; the right-hand traverse puts you below the next thin cracks.
Climb the thin crack to a fixed pin, then make a delicate 15-ft traverse left to a second thin crack, where the first cam goes in blind before the move. Follow the crack to a roomy ledge.
A full rope length: up a chimney and then blocky ground to a tree belay beneath the Hercules Tower.

A varied pitch. Take the ramp right to a steep wall and a left-sweeping crack that widens from 2 to 4 inches where it turns vertical (5.10a; a #4 cam is the one place it is really useful). Over the bulge, follow a ramp to a 5.10a slab traverse right to a thin crack, and climb it on fingertips to a jug, the pitch's crux.
Climb a hand crack, move right around the crest, and follow flakes to a ledge. This pitch and the next easy chimney can be run together as one.
An easy chimney leads to a large ledge of blocks.

Strong hand jams and some stemming up a short, steep face, then traverse right along a narrow ledge and climb blocks to a huge ledge. The stemming section is also graded 5.10a and is the last hard move of the route.

Pass through a hole and go right over the crest to a big ledge, then simul-climb mostly low- to mid-fifth-class ground, staying on or right of the crest. Many options exist and the upper rock is less travelled and lower quality than below, so it can feel ambiguous; keep heading up. A 5.10a hand crack is an optional finish near the top.
